questions.prompt: Which observation best matches cardiac arrest?

choices.text: The casualty is unconscious and is not breathing normally
The casualty is awake and reports ankle pain
The casualty is asleep and breathing normally
The casualty is conscious and coughing

questions.explanation: Cardiac arrest causes loss of consciousness and absence of normal breathing because the heart has stopped pumping blood effectively.

questions.prompt: A casualty is unresponsive and gasping. How should the gasping be interpreted?

As proof that normal breathing has returned
As a reason to delay assessment for one minute

questions.explanation: Gasping is not normal breathing. An unresponsive casualty who is gasping should be treated as being in cardiac arrest.

Leave the casualty and make the call from another room
End the call as soon as the number connects
Wait for an AED before calling

40 to 60 compressions per minute

Hold both pads firmly against the chest
Continue moving the casualty
Disconnect the pads

Whether an AED was used

choices.text: The heart stops pumping blood effectively
The heart pumps faster while circulation remains normal
Only blood flow to the legs stops
Blood flow is unaffected

A heart attack only affects breathing, while cardiac arrest only affects digestion
Cardiac arrest always leaves the casualty conscious

questions.explanation: A heart attack results from coronary-artery blockage and can deteriorate into cardiac arrest, in which the heart stops pumping blood.

sourceReferences.section: 1.4 What Happens in a Heart Attack
1.5 What Happens in a Cardiac Arrest

questions.prompt: Which can be warning signs of a heart attack? Select all that apply.

Sudden breathlessness
Sweating, nausea, vomiting or dizziness

Unconsciousness with no normal breathing as the defining presentation

sourceReferences.section: 1.4 What Happens in a Heart Attack

questions.prompt: Why is immediate action important after cardiac arrest?

choices.text: Brain cells can begin dying within about four to six minutes
There is always at least one hour before injury begins
Delay improves the chance of spontaneous recovery
Time has no effect on survival

questions.explanation: Without restored circulation, brain cells begin dying within roughly four to six minutes, so prompt action matters.

choices.text: About 7 to 10 per cent
Less than 0.1 per cent
Exactly 25 per cent
Survival does not fall

questions.explanation: For untreated ventricular fibrillation, survival falls by about 7 to 10 per cent for each minute of delay.

questions.prompt: What proportion of Singapore's recorded out-of-hospital cardiac arrests in 2019 occurred at home?

choices.text: About 74 per cent
About 10 per cent
About 25 per cent
All cases

questions.prompt: What does the Prevention concept emphasise?

choices.text: Healthy living and regular health checks can reduce risk
Waiting for symptoms before considering health
Using an AED on every conscious person
Avoiding all physical activity

questions.explanation: Prevention concerns reducing risk through a healthy lifestyle and regular check-ups.

Wait silently for someone else to notice
Delay calling until after the third AED analysis
Drive the casualty to hospital before calling

questions.prompt: Why should Early CPR begin promptly?

choices.text: Brain cells can begin dying within four to six minutes
It guarantees that an AED will not be needed
It replaces the need to call 995

Immediate removal of all medical follow-up
AED analysis without pads
Delaying transport for several hours

questions.explanation: Recovery includes community and medical rehabilitation support for a survivor.

Delayed CPR without arranging an AED
Waiting for the casualty to recover without intervention
Defibrillation without first applying pads

Shout for help and call 995

Shake the casualty violently by the neck
Wait quietly without touching or speaking
Press on the abdomen

questions.prompt: A lone rescuer has a handphone beside an unresponsive casualty. What is the correct call flow?

Text a friend and wait for a reply
Walk away before making any call
Call only after the casualty starts breathing normally

questions.prompt: Which breathing-check responses are correct? Select all that apply.

Treat gasping as abnormal breathing and begin CPR

Treat gasping as proof that CPR is unnecessary

questions.explanation: Check for no more than ten seconds. Gasping is not normal breathing; normal breathing means monitoring rather than starting compressions.

questions.prompt: What surface and position are needed for effective CPR?

choices.text: The casualty on their back on a firm, flat surface
The casualty seated upright on a soft sofa
The casualty standing against a wall
The casualty face down on a mattress

questions.explanation: Effective CPR requires the casualty to lie on their back on a firm, flat surface.

questions.prompt: Where should adult chest compressions be delivered?

choices.text: At the centre of the chest over the lower half of the sternum, avoiding the xiphoid process
Directly over the xiphoid process
Over the left collarbone
Over the abdomen below the ribs

questions.explanation: Use the lower half of the sternum at the centre of the chest and avoid the xiphoid process.

questions.prompt: Which description matches adult hand and body position for compressions?

choices.text: One hand heel on the lower sternum, the other on top, fingers interlaced and lifted, elbows straight, shoulders above the chest
Both palms flat on the abdomen with elbows bent
Fingertips on the collarbone with shoulders behind the hips
One hand over the xiphoid process and the other on the neck

questions.explanation: Correct positioning uses stacked hand heels on the lower sternum, interlaced lifted fingers, straight elbows and shoulders directly above the chest.

questions.prompt: What adult compression-depth range is stated in the source?

choices.text: At least 4 cm and not more than 6 cm
1 to 2 cm
Exactly 8 cm
More than 10 cm

questions.prompt: Which statements describe supported compression rhythm and recoil? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Use a rate of 100 to 120 compressions per minute
Allow full recoil after every compression
Keep the hand heels in contact with the chest between compressions
Use fewer than 40 compressions per minute
Lean continuously so the chest cannot recoil

questions.explanation: Use 100 to 120 compressions per minute and allow complete recoil while keeping the hand heels in contact with the chest.

questions.prompt: Which rules correctly limit interruptions or define when CPR stops? Select all that apply.

choices.text: A tired lone rescuer may rest for no more than ten seconds, preferably after about 100 compressions
Pause when the AED prompts analysis, charging or shock
Stop when paramedics take over or the casualty wakes or resumes normal breathing
Take an unrestricted break after every ten compressions

questions.explanation: Keep interruptions brief. The supported stop conditions are emergency-team takeover, AED analysis/charging/shock prompts, or the casualty waking or regaining normal breathing.

questions.prompt: What does an AED do?

choices.text: It analyses the heart rhythm, decides whether a shock is needed and guides the rescuer
It shocks every casualty as soon as it is opened
It replaces the need for chest compressions
It measures blood pressure without pads

questions.explanation: An AED analyses rhythm through its pads, charges only for a shockable rhythm, and gives voice guidance to the rescuer.

questions.prompt: Which AED hazards must be made safe? Select all that apply.

Contact with a metal surface
Flammable gas or an oxygen source nearby
A dry, non-metallic surface with no flammable source nearby
A bare, dry chest on which the pads can adhere

questions.explanation: Address wet conditions, metal contact and flammable gases or oxygen sources before AED use.

Apply pads over a wet chest

Open the AED box
Power on the AED
Prepare the chest
Apply the right pad
Apply the left pad

Let the AED analyse and keep everyone clear
